meta.title: A Single Reason To Not Vibe Code
meta.author: asindu

comments.author: orib
comments.text: AI coding is passive consumption cosplaying as making something. Any place where you're actually producing something yourself is a bug in the product.

comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text:
I think this reduces AI to one totally inaccurate dimension. You can build an app with a prompt as simple as "built me an app." Or, you can provide an extremely detailed specification controlling every facet of the design. Or, you can work iteratively, and create prototypes to get a feel for what works and what doesn't work for a particular app.

Each of these provides totally different levels of "atrophy."

comments.author: creesch
comments.text:
You can build an app with a prompt as simple as "built me an app." Or, you can provide an extremely detailed specification controlling every facet of the design. Or, you can work iteratively, and create prototypes to get a feel for what works and what doesn't work for a particular app.


This is entirely true. But, it does require you to make that choice and keep making that choice. Something that can be surprisingly difficult as many people (I'd say most if not all) people tend to automatically go for things that are easier to do.

I fully agree that there are different levels of "atrophy", but a lot of people might not even realize or give thought to this and to what degree.


Or, you can provide an extremely detailed specification controlling every facet of the design.


For example, I'd say that this still falls within the spectrum of "lazy" usage of these models where atrophy of your skills can easily happen over time. You can only give these extremely detail specifications and excerpt control if you have that knowledge and working experience. As soon as you stop practicing that experience it might make you less capable over time to do the same thing to the same degree of quality. Which is something I have seen happen outside of LLM usage plenty of times with developers who transition to more abstract roles like tech leads (depending on how the role works in the company), architects, etc.

I also think that all three of your examples still pretty much lean into the generative way of using LLMs where the probability of atrophy, in my opinion, is highest. It is still entirely possible to use LLMs as tools external to the process, get a benefit from them and keep your brain sharp. Where you use them as interactive rubber duckies, do some sanity checks on code you wrote, etc.

What is important to recognize here though, that is not what the massive hype is trying to get you to do and what most people are likely to try out these days. The hype train (choo choo) is full on trying to sell the notion that LLMs can do ALL THE THINGS basically from scratch and that people should lean as much into agentic workflows as possible. Which, in the context of this post, I think is extremely harmful for the short and long term future of many developers.

Edit: I saw some other comments shrugging of the atrophy of skills saying you can still keep your brain engaged in other ways. Which is entirely true, but also overlooks a point I consider fairly important. Unless you truly don't care about the quality of the end product you will need the skills and insights to validate LLM output.

comments.author: nextos
comments.text:
Going in the same direction, I think it's nice to consider using a purely functional language, ideally with strong types. One can guide the design, and work on one function at a time. One can get help from an LLM to code the current function, just like some theorem provers were already doing two decades ago [1].

Advantages: the LLM doesn't need to deal with context, and one still controls the entire process, but from time to time one can get implementation ideas from the machine.

[1] https://hackage.haskell.org/package/djinn

comments.author: amw-zero
comments.text:
I don’t think this currently scales to any practical system.

But, interestingly, LLMs seem to report statically typed languages, especially with effect systems, as their ideal target. Since they are not sentient (I don’t believe they are), this is really just a reflection of people’s beliefs about PLs in general. But I do think it makes sense - local reasoning is a super power for LLMs.

comments.author: dysoco
comments.text:
There are many ways to keep your brain engaged that are not writing code at your day job, you could for example play Sudoku, Factorio or hell even code yourself a hobby project without any side help.

Speaking of day jobs, I don't think "thinking"is going anyway, sure you might get rusty in writing code but that's not going to be so relevant in the future anymore (sadly). You will probably get to do a lot of brain-intensive work such as technical writing, defining and solving problems, discussing with peers, etc.

So yes, your ability to write code is going to become hampered, but that doesn't imply your brain will atrophy completely, there are many other activities you can do.

As for the London cab driver thing... well perhaps my city cab driver is happy that he doesn't have to study all the streets once he arrives home, and he can rest instead.

comments.author: repl
comments.text:
This is not an abuse of the spam flag. Community moderation works precisely because people are allowed to vote and flag based on their judgment. In this case, 18 people upvoted the post, but 8 people flagged it as spam. That means nearly 30% of voters felt it is spam. Even if that's a minority view, it's a significant one. It shouldn't be dismissed simply by litigating what "spam" means.

A growing portion of the community is frustrated with the steady stream of low-effort posts that rehash the same points over and over. The vibecoding tag in particular has become full of repetitive, shallow, and often self-promotional content. The tag is losing its usefulness. These posts don't make me a better programmer in anyway (one of the community posting criteria). These posts make me want to tear my hair out.

I don’t want to mute the vibecoding tag entirely, because thoughtful and genuinely insightful posts do occasionally appear there. But the pattern of low-effort, repetitive submissions that seem designed more for visibility than for meaningful discussion is really taking a toll on the community. When the same shallow takes show up day after day, it degrades the signal-to-noise ratio for everyone.

Imagine if someone posted daily about how great (or terrible) Vim is, generating predictable upvotes and discussion each time. Even if some people upvoted those posts, over time it would feel exhausting. That's what is happening with vibecoding tag today.

One of the reasons I’ve always valued this forum is the consistently thoughtful, high-signal discussions. When a tag becomes an endless stream of repetitive, low-effort content, it degrades what makes this community special. I am going to be flagging every such self-promotional, low effort post (vibecoding or otherwise) to make my voice heard.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Yeah, this is the "skills atrophy" concern.

Letting your skills atrophy is a choice. If you're mindful about how you use these new tools you can use them to boost your skills instead.

comments.author: jcd
comments.text:
I actually don't think it's a choice. Practice and habit produce competency. If you stop doing the things that produce competency, you lose it. LLMs will have an effect on competency that is somewhere between digital calculators and written language.

You, as someone who developed their skills before these tools were available, may choose a subset of your skills to keep sharp, and jettison the ones you don't think are valuable anymore, but there's a limited amount of time to do things each day and you will get out of practice in the things you choose to no longer do.

"But LLMs enable people to do so much more!" someone might retort, so they have more time to hone skills. This may prove true, but I have might doubts: the growing reports of mental exhaustion from LLM enthusiasts indicate the mental context switching is not without cost.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
Practice and habit produce competency. If you stop doing the things that produce competency, you lose it.


That's what I mean by "it's a choice". You need to decide which things you want to achieve competency at and invest time in those things, even when there's a less time consuming option available to you.

Making those choices isn't easy, and requires discipline. Being the kind of person who thinks about skill atrophy is an excellent first step!

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
The writing comparison is a really good one.

One of my biggest concerns around LLMs and education is that students are using them to write essays.

I firmly believe that writing is a skill you gain through tedium. You have to write a lot in order to get competent. And writing is both thinking and communication, so it's important to build those muscles.

If you get AI to write everything for you during those formative years it's going to really hurt you.

I learned to program 20+ years ago so I'm completely out of touch with what it takes to start down that path. Could it be that it's like writing in that without the tedium you never develop the critical mental muscles you need?

comments.author: fbegyn
comments.text:
I think writing is an excellent comparison for this. Because writing is something where we have already seen this massive improvement and the effect on cognitive learning paths.

Mainly hand written > typewriter > computer (> LLM are probably the next iterator). We already have plenty of studies who all (at least in core principle) have proven that the reduction in "tedium" has shown to reduce the retention (which I analogue with learning) capabilities. Mainly proving that with more tedium (hand writing something), retention is greater.

LLMs are the first to make me worry because they completely obsolete the "tedium" part of writing (= writing being the actual act of writing something, not coming up with the idea itself). I wonder if this will completely disintegrate the retention. And we already see idea/concepts shaping (tech debt moving to mental debt, teams vibe coding that lose overview in weeks/months).

comments.author: cole-k
comments.text:
I think I'm with Simon here. Someone will need to explain to me what tedium is exactly being improved upon by using LLMs over e.g. a computer for writing, specifically.

Much of the writing I have done has been about articulating my own thoughts. Now if you don't care about rhetoric or whatnot, then maybe you'd say that this is the tedium LLMs automate. But to only automate rhetoric requires an unreasonable degree of discipline.

I suspect that the way students use LLMs to write is more likely "Does Candide agree with Professor Pangloss that this is 'the best of all possible worlds'?" than "I believe Candide agrees with Professor Pangloss for reasons X, Y, and Z. Please write this in an essay format, keeping my thoughts unchanged but making the writing clear and convincing."

I feel like it's usually a bit drastic to claim someone is outsourcing their own thinking to an LLM, but the first query is very explicitly doing this. And the kicker here is that --- until the neuralink or whatever is perfected --- to get LLMs to do any of our writing, we need to first write to the LLM.

So even in the best possible case where you retain full control of your thoughts and the LLM is just a means for shaping their presentation, the way they're presented is determined by... your writing. I suppose I'll never know if that's a win because it certainly doesn't appeal to me.

comments.author: jcd
comments.text: I think the difference between handwritten, typewritten, word processor-written vs LLMs is the act of attention from the writer. And I know from using spaced repetition that the act of attention is important for retention. With the older ways of doing things, attentive focus was part of producing textual artifacts, but that is no longer a given. There may be ways of getting around this in the new way, but it is not inherent to the work itself. That will have knock-on effects.

comments.author: townley
comments.text:
I'm cautiously hopeful that this isn't the end times of thoughtful craft in code or writing.

Higher-level languages removed the tedium of memory management, frameworks reduced the time needed to configure CORS/escape queries... there's precedent for tedious things becoming automatic, but the tedium--or craft, if you regard it positively--remains.

Maybe agentic coding skills are fundamentally different, and they do compel us to think less. Or maybe (hopefully) they're lego blocks that give new developers starting their 20 year journey a way to tackle tedious problems of a higher order.
